title: Can dot counts alone show equal sides and right angles?
description: A tilted square on a dot grid is tested by counting the dots across and down for each side. The video shows that equal counts give equal sides and swapped counts give right angles. Keeko raises the doubt that only a ruler and a protractor can tell.
teaching_notes: One idea: on a dot grid, the counts across and down from corner to corner decide the lengths and the angles. Watch for children who think a tilted figure can only be judged by measuring.

source: Is it possible to reason out if the sides are equal or not, and if the angles are right or not, without using any measuring instruments? Can we do this by only looking at the position of corners in the dot grid?
video_script.why: The child uses the counts of dots across and down to decide whether the sides are equal and the angles are right angles, with no measuring instrument.
video_script.substitution: A tilted figure PQRS with corners on dots; the moves are three across and two down, then two across and three down.
video_script.anchor: A tilted figure PQRS on a dot grid with every corner on a dot
video_script.wrong_answer: only a ruler and a protractor can tell us
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks only a ruler and a protractor can tell us, as tilted shapes mislead the eye. Counting dots is exact, so the counts do the work of both instruments, and the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, the positions of the dots make it possible.

final_answer.value: yes; the same counts across and down for every side give equal sides, and counts swapped at each turn give right angles
final_answer.spoken: yes, the positions of the dots make it possible; the same counts across and down give equal sides, and counts swapped at each turn give right angles

never_show: the verdict on the figure before the answer
maths_rules: Take P at the top. The corner Q is 3 dots right and 2 dots down from P. The corner R is 2 dots left and 3 dots down from Q. The corner S is 3 dots left and 2 dots up from R. Then P is 2 dots right and 3 dots up from S.
Every side uses the counts 3 and 2, so every side has the same length (the square of that length is 3 x 3 + 2 x 2 = 9 + 4 = 13 square dot steps, but the video only compares the counts).
P to Q is 3 across and 2 down; turning this step by a quarter turn (90 degrees) swaps the counts: Q to R is 2 across and 3 down.
At every corner the next step is the previous step turned a quarter turn, so every angle is 90 degrees.
A rotation keeps lengths, so each turned step is as long as the one before it.
video_script.design: One idea: counts of dots across and down decide equal sides and right angles. Uses rotation keeps lengths and angles. Wrong idea: only measuring instruments can decide. The figure stays all video.
